hints: Look at how much CO2 is made in each 30 s interval, the rate is slowing down, so think about what happens to concentration and collision frequency as reactants are used.
Work out the starting moles of each reactant, 4 g of $\text{CaCO}_3$ and $100 \text{ cm}^3$ of $0.10 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{HCl}$, then use the 1 to 2 ratio in the equation.
Compare the moles needed with the moles available to spot the limiting reactant, that is the one that runs out and makes the gas volume level off.
walkthrough:
**See what the data tells us about rate**

Look at the volume made in each interval. From 0 to 30 s you get 40 cm3, from 30 to 60 s you get 30 cm3, then 18, then 13, then 9, then 6, then 4, then 0.

The extra volume per unit time gets smaller and smaller, so the rate is decreasing with time.

**Explain the slowing rate with collision theory**

As the reaction proceeds, $\text{H}^+$ ions and $\text{CaCO}_3$ particles are consumed, so the concentration of acid falls.

With fewer reactant particles per unit volume, there are fewer successful collisions per second, so the rate falls. This rules out any answer saying more collisions occur.

$$\text{CaCO}_3(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

**Find which reactant runs out first**

Calculate starting moles of each reactant.

Moles of calcium carbonate:
$$n(\text{CaCO}_3) = \frac{4}{100} = 0.040 \text{ mol}$$

Moles of hydrochloric acid:
$$n(\text{HCl}) = \frac{100}{1000} \times 0.10 = 0.010 \text{ mol}$$

**Use the equation ratio to identify the limiting reactant**

The equation needs 2 mol of $\text{HCl}$ for every 1 mol of $\text{CaCO}_3$.

To react all 0.040 mol of $\text{CaCO}_3$ you would need $0.080$ mol of $\text{HCl}$, but you only have $0.010$ mol. So $\text{HCl}$ is in large deficit.

That means the acid is completely used up while lots of solid remains, and when the acid is gone no more $\text{CO}_2$ can form, so the volume levels off at 120 cm3.

options.A: The first half is correct, the rate falls because concentration falls and fewer collisions occur. The second half is wrong because $\text{CaCO}_3$ (0.040 mol) is in large excess over $\text{HCl}$ (0.010 mol), so the solid cannot be the reactant that runs out.
options.B: This is correct on both counts. Rate decreases because reactants are consumed, acid concentration drops, and fewer collisions per second occur. The reaction stops because the limiting reactant $\text{HCl}$ is used up, only 0.010 mol available versus 0.080 mol needed for all the solid.
options.C: Both halves are wrong. Collisions do not increase with time, they decrease as concentration decreases, which is why the volume increments get smaller. $\text{CaCO}_3$ is also in excess, not limiting, so it is not used up.
options.D: The second half correctly identifies $\text{HCl}$ as the limiting reactant that is used up. The first half is wrong because the rate slows down, it does not speed up, so collision frequency must be decreasing, not increasing.
